clusters.name: Your grandfather Clifford's return and your time at the conservatory, 1989–1992
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather's return to the family in early 1989, within months your family moved houses twice and you settled into the rebuilt Hollin Road with your mother and Desmond. Your late nights began that autumn; you leaned hard on your roommate Rafe once you started at Wexley Conservatory in the fall of 1991, but when you hurt your wrist weeks into your first term you lost your footing—anxious, unable to function, your closest friendship blew up, and you were on your own getting high and absorbed in radios by November. Your grandfather Gordon died in June 1991, caught in the same months: with him gone and your mother about to remarry, you say you had no footing. The shifts pile up from the move through the wrist injury and its aftermath, each one near another's.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's cancer diagnosis and your move away, 2001–2003
clusters.reason: Around the time your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, you were running out of steam for performing and your audition for the national orchestra failed; you were on poor terms with your parents and moved away from Thornbury to Gull Harbour, then followed Marisol to Fenwick. When you and Marisol split within the year you sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury; you could not face your parents and relied on friends instead. You say you were lost and low with no footing, as in the first stretch. The shifts cluster around the months when your grandmother's illness was running and your own collapse gathered speed.

clusters.name: Wren's marriage to you and her family's closeness, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, within the months that followed you saw your mother a bit less; by October 2019 she was swamped with one thing after another—her family's street party, a fundraising dinner, the drive to the lake for her mother's retirement. You overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her; she talks with her father and brother all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. At the lake weekend you awoke from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose; your sleep is at its worst around her family and you feel you don't belong. The shifts in your relationship with your partner and in your own anxiety and sleep pile up across these years, each one tied to her family's demands and closeness.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
